publicKnowledge.title: Car knowledge should be public knowledge.
publicKnowledge.body: Everyone gets taken advantage of at some point: first-time buyers, seasoned ones, people paying cash, people financing. VINdicated translates the dealer playbook into plain language, from inspection checklists to financing explainers to the scripts that get you out of a pressure sale, so you can walk in alone and walk out with a fair deal.

footing.title: Nobody walks in on equal footing.
footing.body: The price you get depends on who's asking, and new tools are making it easier than ever to take advantage of buyers.

rows.title: Same car. Same script. Different price.
rows.body: Black male car buyers were quoted prices averaging $1,100 higher than white male buyers for identical cars, using identical bargaining scripts. Black women were quoted $410 more than white men, and white women $92 more.
rows.cite: Ayres & Siegelman, The American Economic Review, 1995

rows.title: Financed for a car that never existed.
rows.body: A careful buyer found a fairly priced truck on Facebook Marketplace, from what looked like a real Texas dealer. The paperwork, the bank approval, even a live delivery tracker all checked out. The dealer was an AI-assisted clone, and the truck was never real.

rows.title: Longer at the table, worse at the counter.
rows.body: Dealers spent 13% longer negotiating with minority testers and made racist or sexist comments in 4% of test visits. In a separate study, 63% of non-white testers were given worse pricing than white testers.
rows.cite: Ayres & Siegelman, 1995 · National Fair Housing Alliance, 2018

strikes.title: Vindicated from what?
strikes.body: Three strikes. Three completely different situations. The same system every time.

items.title: The Pink Slip Scam
paras: At 18, I was trying to buy a car from my friend's dad. He made me wait three months, promising the whole time to sell it to me.
When the time finally came, he tried to tell me I didn't need the pink slip. He was trying to scam me. Without the title in your name, the car is not legally yours, no matter what you paid.

items.title: Facebook Marketplace
paras: I tried buying a car on Facebook Marketplace. The conversation started normally with mileage, price, when I could come look.
As soon as he found out I was female, the tone shifted completely. He told me, "Shut your mouth, bitch," and blocked me.
After that, I made a fake Facebook account under the name Randall, and had my brother call sellers on my behalf. I got better deals when they thought they were dealing with a man.

items.title: South Coast Mitsubishi
paras: I test drove a car alone. When I came back with my sister to buy it, it suddenly read: "Buy today or lose it." They promised a 300-point inspection. Then 150. Then the service records were in a locked drawer.
They handed me a financing contract with 30% APR on a cash deal and pointed to an arbitration agreement when I asked how it would be voided.

story.subtitle: Three strikes. Three completely different situations. The same system every time.

strikes.label: The Pink Slip Scam
body: At 18, I was trying to buy a car from my friend's dad. He made me wait three months, promising the whole time to sell it to me.
When the time finally came, he tried to tell me I didn't need the pink slip. He was trying to scam me. Without the title in your name, the car is not legally yours, no matter what you paid.

strikes.label: Facebook Marketplace
body: I tried buying a car on Facebook Marketplace. The conversation started normally with mileage, price, when I could come look.
As soon as he found out I was female, the tone shifted completely. He told me, "Shut your mouth, bitch," and blocked me.
After that, I made a fake Facebook account under the name Randall, and had my brother call sellers on my behalf. I got better deals when they thought they were dealing with a man.

strikes.label: South Coast Mitsubishi
body: April 2025. I test drove a car alone. When I came back with my sister to buy it, it suddenly read: "Buy today or lose it." I asked for service records. I was told they were in a locked drawer, and the guy with the key wasn't there. They promised a 300-point inspection. Then 150. Then it was back in the locked drawer.
I paid for an independent inspection at a Toyota dealership. They found issues. When I drove back, there was a rattling noise. Eddy told me I broke the car during the test drive.

They handed me a financing contract with 30% APR. I was paying cash. "Sign this until you bring a cashier's check." I asked where it said the contract would be voided. He pointed to an arbitration agreement. I took business law. I know what arbitration means. He got angry. I said, "I know you're frustrated." He said, "You would be correct," and left.

pullquote.quote: I reported Eddy. When the GM called to apologize, I said, "I don't accept your apology. I hope whether a 19-year-old girl or a 50-year-old man walks in, you'll treat everyone with respect."

Rana Darwich.bio: Rana Darwich is a student researcher at UC Berkeley and the Founder & President of VINdicated, which now runs chapters at UCLA, Berkeley, and UC Santa Cruz. She is a Research Assistant at UC Berkeley's School of Education studying gender equity in university athletics funding, a Research Apprentice at Berkeley Law's Center for Comparative Inequality and Anti-Discrimination Law, and a former Student Researcher at the Political Violence Lab. She previously interned at Amazon and is currently an Opinion writer at The Daily Californian.

Fiona Wangsawidjaja.bio: Fiona Wangsawidjaja is a Statistics and Data Science major at UCLA and the current President of the UCLA VINdicated chapter. Fiona loves to educate and help her community when she can, whether through her past experience as a coding tutor, helping others learn about the digital world through conferences, or here at VINdicated, where she hopes people can benefit from accessible automotive literacy. She has experience specializing in data through organizations such as DataRes and NSDC, teaching high school students about data, building data analysis projects, and consulting companies.

Ashwin Vinod.bio: Ashwin Vinod is a Computer Science major at UCSC. He is the President of the VINdicated chapter at UCSC. Through involvement in various research labs and software engineering experiences, Ashwin has built a technical foundation that he wants to use to push computational research that benefits the community, and provide educational opportunities for his community. Ashwin previously interned at IBM as a Software Developer Intern, and is continuing his interest in research as part of the AIEA Lab @ UCSC, focused on explainable artificial intelligence.

Rizwaan Bana.bio: Rizwaan Bana is a Computer Science major at UCLA. He is the Chapter Director at VINdicated @ UCLA, where he helps streamline the chapters' outreach and project strategies. He also serves as the Internal Vice President of Bruin Software Engineers, Dev Team Project Manager for ACM @ UCLA, and Web Chair for UPE @ UCLA.

William Prawira.bio: Will Prawira is a Math & Data Science major at UCLA and the Internal VP of the VINdicated chapter there. With his background in data science and industry experience, Will hopes to push a culture of rapid, high-quality execution, turning ambitious ideas into valuable resources for the community. He is currently interning at Navitas Semiconductor through the academic year as a Reliability Intern, where he develops tools and applications focused on automation and product lifetime prediction modeling.

Ayat Ashraf.bio: Ayat Ashraf is a Math/Econ major at UCLA interested in economic policymaking. She does research at VINdicated, so she can hopefully buy a car without calling her dad 8,000 times in the future.

Noirit Ghosh Choudhuri.bio: Noirit Ghosh Choudhuri is a Computer Science major at UC Berkeley. He is the Internal Vice President of the VINdicated chapter at UC Berkeley. Through his experience developing multiple real world projects, Noirit has built strong technical and collaborative skills that he wants to use to build more solutions to pressing societal issues, such as the one VINdicated stands to fight.

Halima Cherif Hminat.bio: Halima Cherif Hminat is an Integrative Biology student at UC Berkeley, minoring in Sustainable Business and Policy, and is on the pre-dental track. She is also the EVP at VINdicated @ UC Berkeley and contributes to creating resources that help people make informed decisions with confidence. She says VINdicated's mission is important because she wants to support women by helping them prevent unfair treatment in car buying and repairs.

Gundeep Sambee.bio: Gundeep is a Cognitive Science student at UC Santa Cruz, minoring in Technology and Information Management. She's interested in the intersection of people and technology, especially how AI, design, and psychology shape the way we make decisions. Outside class, she's involved in research and enjoys opportunities to learn more about human behavior and cognition, and likes taking on leadership roles that build community and create meaningful experiences for others.

Adhya Maddukuri.bio: Adhya is a Technology and Information Management student at UC Santa Cruz with a passion for building technology that creates real-world impact, spanning software development, AI, data analytics, and product strategy. She's conducted undergraduate research in generative AI, consulted with nonprofits through 180 Degrees Consulting, and helped organize hackathons with NVIDIA and ASUS. She's currently a Software Development Engineering Intern at Heron Power, building software systems and strengthening her technical and problem-solving skills.

Fernando Cedillo-Hernandez.bio: Fernando Cedillo-Hernandez is a Biology and Political Science double major at UCLA, with minors in Biomedical Research and Community Engagement and Social Change. He brings a background in research and civic advocacy to his role as Research Lead at VINdicated, driven by a commitment to expanding equitable access and protection for underserved communities. Outside VINdicated, Fernando is involved in leadership and community engagement work across UCLA, including advocacy for immigrant and working-class students.

Yinrui (Ray) Gan.bio: Ray Gan leads the data and AI pipeline for VINdicated's interactive dealership risk map. He designed the LLM-based classification system that turns unstructured consumer reviews into transparent, evidence-backed risk signals for car buyers. Ray studies Computer Science and Linguistics at UCLA.

Evanceline Tang.bio: Evanceline is a second year biology major at UCLA. She is passionate about using art and design as a mean of conveying messages. Through her art, she hopes to help people understand more about VINdicated and the existing inequalities and dangers in the automotive industry.

Rouqaya Elbanna.bio: Rouqaya Elbanna is a high school student and the HS Lead at VINdicated, where she works to bring the organization's consumer protection mission to a wider student audience. She previously served as Vice President of TEDxAIS Jeddah Youth and was selected for the Learn with Leaders Future Doctors Fellowship, where her capstone health education campaign on Alzheimer's caregiving earned Best Presentation of the cohort. An aspiring physician, Rouqaya also competes as a varsity volleyball athlete and was honored with her school's Female Scholar Athlete Award.

Daryen Romero.bio: Daryen Romero is a Computer Science student at UC Berkeley. Joining VINdicated is important to him because he wants to help others be informed about the importance of buying a car and not be afraid. He also wants to speak out and help others understand how people can be taken advantage of if they are a woman or a different race.

Vanessa Phan.bio: Vanessa is pursuing a degree in Computer Engineering with a concentration in Computer Systems, interested in the combination of software and electrical engineering, especially robotics and intelligent technologies. She's the Treasurer for the Society of Women Engineers at UC Santa Cruz, where she's secured more than $5,000 in funding this year, and has been involved in SlothLab as a developer. She wants to get more involved in research, digging into topics in detail and applying what she learns to build solutions.

Brisa Gómez.bio: Brisa Gómez is a fourth-year Psychology major at UCLA and the Technical Writing Lead at UCLA. Through their involvement in various writing and translation projects, Brisa wants to use that experience to promote accessible and comprehensive resources that are inclusive to vulnerable populations.

Pierce Kosobayashi.bio: Pierce Kosobayashi is a fourth-year Media Studies and Education student at UC Berkeley. He brings a background in digital and retail automotive sales and finance, along with experience in OEM sales analysis and marketing, to his work as Project Manager at VINdicated. A car enthusiast at heart, Pierce wants to use his industry experience to help future buyers navigate the process with confidence. Outside VINdicated, he enjoys ocean swimming, hiking, and spending time with his dog and cat.

Chino Sawatyanont.bio: Chino is an Electrical and Computer Engineering major at UC Berkeley and a Software Engineer for the VINdicated chapter there. He brings extensive experience combining technical knowledge with societal impact, having previously focused on supporting underprivileged communities in Thailand. Chino hopes to bring that same drive for impact to VINdicated's mission.

William Guo.bio: William Guo is a junior studying Computer Science at UC Santa Cruz and a Software Engineer at VINdicated. He enjoys tinkering with and fixing electronics, playing video games, and getting hands-on with his own projects. Having gone through the stressful process of searching for the right vehicle himself, William resonates deeply with VINdicated's mission and believes the basics of what to look for in a major purchase like a car should be more readily available to everyone.

Daniel.bio: Daniel is a transfer Applied Math student from Los Angeles and Data Engineer at VINdicated, with a strong interest in personal finance and teaching financial literacy to others. Outside of VINdicated, he enjoys tearing down and repairing computers, hiking, cycling, and running around the city. He's also gotten into climbing, cooking, and going to music festivals.

Chloe Lin.bio: Chloe Lin is an Integrative Biology student at UC Berkeley serving as Outreach Lead at VINdicated. Her experience advocating for women and underrepresented communities drives her commitment to bridging knowledge gaps in the automotive industry. She is dedicated to empowering everyday consumers to navigate car purchases and maintenance with clarity and confidence.

Ian de la Houssaye.bio: Ian de la Houssaye is a Mechanical Engineering student and the Software Lead for the VINdicated chapter at UC Berkeley. He has a passion for building technology that solves real-world problems. Ian founded and led his high school's competitive robotics team, helping it become one of San Diego's top-performing teams while directing the development of its software and autonomous systems. Through these experiences, he has developed strong technical, leadership, and collaborative skills that he hopes to use to advance VINdicated's mission.

James Cheng.bio: James is a Data Science and Cognitive Science student at UC Berkeley and a Data Engineer at VINdicated. He brings extensive experience in both STEM and language education, along with a diverse technical background and experience building independent projects. He hopes to draw on these experiences to bring a unique perspective and strong initiative to solving problems in the automotive industry.

Bryan Zhang.bio: Bryan Zhang is a CS major at UCLA. In his free time he enjoys playing basketball, volleyball, and baking. He is a developer for VINdicated.

Rahul Puritipati.bio: Rahul Puritipati is a first-year CS student at UCLA. Raised in Folsom, CA, he likes to watch gym TikToks and be a couch GM for the 49ers and Kings. He has done a significant amount of nonprofit work, mainly rebuilding local businesses' online presence and raising money for underprivileged youth in India.

Jordan Acle.bio: Jordan Acle is a Data Science student at UC Berkeley and the Data Lead for the VINdicated chapter there, bringing hands-on experience in machine learning, data analysis, and data engineering to the role. He currently works as a Product Strategy Intern at Innov8AI, contributing to a trust-centered health AI platform, and serves UC Berkeley's community as a Data Science Peer Advisor and Hello World Mentor, helping new students build confidence and find their footing on campus.

hero.title: Don't buy a car without this.
hero.body: A pre-purchase inspection (PPI) is the single most important thing you can do before buying a used car. It costs $100–200 and can save you thousands.

what.title: What is a pre-purchase inspection?
body: A PPI is when you pay an
, not the seller, not the dealership, to inspect a car before you buy it. A good PPI costs
and is the single most powerful tool you have before signing anything.
what.notTitle: A PPI is not the same as

nots.title: The seller's inspection
nots.body: They're trying to sell you the car.

nots.title: A test drive
nots.body: You can't see what's happening under the hood.

engine.title: Inspect it yourself.
engine.body: Tap any glowing part, or start a guided inspection. We'll zoom in, walk you through the check, and keep score as you go.
engine.imageAlt: Illustrated engine bay with labeled parts including the fuse box, intake air tube, brake fluid reservoir, spark plugs, battery, coolant reservoir, radiator, and fan
engine.doneBody: You've checked all 9. Anything you flagged is a question for your mechanic, or a reason to negotiate.

parts.sub: The box that keeps the car's electricity safe
parts.what: The fuse box holds small safety pieces called fuses that protect every electrical circuit. If something goes wrong, a fuse blows to stop damage, like a safety switch.
steps: Ask to open the lid. Look for blown fuses; the metal strip inside will be broken.
Look for mismatched fuses. A 30-amp fuse in a 10-amp slot means someone bypassed an electrical problem, which is dangerous.
Check for burn marks, melting, or a burnt smell.
Look for dirt, water stains, or rust. The inside should be clean and dry.
Check for messy, taped, or spliced wiring. Clean factory wiring is normal.
parts.flag: Red flag: blown or mismatched fuses, burn marks, or messy wiring mean existing electrical problems, some of the hardest and most expensive to diagnose on a used car.

parts.what: The big ribbed tube carries air from the air filter box into the engine. Inside that box, a paper or foam filter keeps dust and debris out.
steps: Look along the tube for cracks, splits, or loose clamps.
Find the filter box the tube connects to and open it if you can (usually 2 to 4 clips).
Hold the filter up to the light. Clean is light gray or white; dirty is dark gray or black.
parts.flag: A badly clogged filter on a car with "full service history" is a red flag: the records are incomplete, or the seller is exaggerating. Filters cost $15 to $30 and should be replaced every 15,000 to 30,000 miles.

parts.what: This translucent tank feeds the brakes. Brake fluid absorbs moisture over time, which quietly weakens braking.
steps: Read the level through the side of the tank. It should sit between MIN and MAX.
Check the color. Clear to light amber is healthy; dark brown means it's overdue.
A low level can mean worn brake pads or a leak. Ask when the brakes were last serviced.
On the test drive, the pedal should feel firm, not soft or spongy.
parts.flag: Red flag: a spongy pedal, or fluid that's dark and low, means brake work before you buy. Brakes are never a place to cut corners.

parts.what: Spark plugs ignite the fuel in each cylinder. On most modern engines they sit under ignition coils, the red boots on top of this engine.
steps: Look at the coil boots for cracks or damage.
Ask your mechanic to check for oil pooling in the spark plug wells, a sign of a leaking gasket.
On the test drive, notice any rough idle, shaking, or hesitation when you accelerate.
Ask when the plugs were last replaced. Many are due somewhere around 60,000 to 100,000 miles.
parts.flag: A misfire or oil in the plug wells is a repair item you can negotiate on. A flashing check engine light means an active misfire: stop the test drive.

parts.sub: Open this: what's inside tells you a lot
parts.what: The oil filler cap is where new oil goes in. It takes two seconds to open, and what you see inside tells you things the dipstick alone cannot.
steps: Twist it counterclockwise and lift off. Look at the underside of the cap and inside the opening.
Look for any white or cream-colored residue, froth, or buildup.
Smell inside briefly. It should smell like oil, nothing chemical or sweet.
parts.flag: Serious red flag: white or creamy residue that looks like mayonnaise is oil mixing with coolant, often from a blown head gasket. That repair can exceed $3,000. Walk away or negotiate hard.
parts.flag2: Also watch for: thick, tar-like sludge. It means the engine went long stretches without oil changes, which shortens its life.

parts.sub: Corrosion tells the story. So does the date.
parts.what: The 12-volt battery powers the starter and all the electronics. Most last 3 to 5 years, and replacement runs $100 to $250.
steps: Look for a date sticker on the top or side.
Check the terminals for white, blue, or green fuzzy corrosion.
Look at the case for bulging, cracks, or leaks.
parts.flag: Red flags: heavy corrosion, a battery 4+ years old, or a bulging case. A visibly old battery is a fair $150 to $250 ask off the price.

parts.sub: Never open when hot. Read it cold.
parts.what: The coolant reservoir is a translucent plastic tank that holds the engine's coolant. You can read it without opening anything.
steps: Look through the side of the tank to see the level.
Check that it sits between the MIN and MAX marks.
Look at the color. Coolant should be bright green, orange, pink, or blue.
Only open the cap if the engine is completely cold. Hot coolant under pressure can cause serious burns.
parts.flag: Red flags: brown or rusty coolant means neglect. Milky or foamy coolant means oil has mixed in, a head gasket failure costing $1,500 to $3,000+.

parts.what: The serpentine belt drives the alternator, power steering, AC, and water pump. If it breaks while driving, you lose all of them at once.
steps: With the engine off, find the wide, flat ribbed belt looping around several pulleys at the front of the engine.
Look at the ribbed side. Fine cracks between the ribs are the first sign of aging.
Check the smooth back side. A glazed, shiny look means it's slipping.
Ask your mechanic to estimate how much life is left.
parts.flag: Price impact: a new belt costs $75 to $200 installed. If it looks worn, use it to negotiate; it isn't a deal-breaker.

parts.sub: The system that keeps the engine from overheating
parts.what: The radiator sits at the very front. Hot coolant flows through it, and air through its fins cools it before it heads back to the engine. The fan pulls extra air through when the car is sitting still.
steps: With the engine cold, look for bent fins, cracks, or dried green, orange, or pink residue.
Check around the base and hoses for wet spots or coolant stains.
Start the engine and let it idle a few minutes. The fan should kick on.
Watch the temperature gauge on the test drive. It should stay in the normal range.
parts.flag: Red flag: any coolant leak is a repair before purchase. A cracked radiator runs $300 to $900, and overheating on the test drive is a serious warning.

where.title: Where to get a PPI.

cards.title: Independent inspection services
paras: (carchex.com): Mobile or shop-based, detailed report. Cost: $100–200.

cards.title: Manufacturer dealerships
paras: If you're buying a used Honda from a Mitsubishi dealership,

paras.b: take it to a Honda dealership for the PPI.

paras: They know that brand inside and out, have the right diagnostic equipment, and have zero incentive to lie. Cost: usually $100–150.

cards.title: AAA membership
paras: Many AAA locations offer free or discounted PPIs for members. Check your local AAA auto service center.

cards.title: Trusted local mechanics
paras: If you have a mechanic you trust, ask if they do PPIs. Red flags: they refuse to put findings in writing, they rush through it, or they tell you "everything looks fine" without checking anything.

where.dealersBody: Buying a used Honda from a Mitsubishi dealer? Take it to a Honda dealership for your PPI.

checks.title: Why you're paying for your safety.
checks.body: A good inspector goes through the car systematically. Here's what they're checking, and why each category matters.

items.title: Engine: the heart of the car
points: Is oil dripping from the engine? Small leaks become big repairs.
Overheating can destroy an engine quickly and expensively.
If this snaps while driving, your engine could be totaled.
Even if the light isn't on, a mechanic can pull stored codes.
Reveals internal engine wear that visual inspection can't catch.

items.title: Transmission: often the most expensive fix
items.intro: Transmission repairs can cost $3,000–$8,000. An inspector checks for:
points: Smooth gear shifts (automatics and manuals)
Fluid condition and color (should be clear pink or red, not brown or burnt)
Slipping between gears under acceleration
Unusual sounds during gear changes

items.title: Brakes: non-negotiable safety
points: Under 3mm means immediate replacement.
Scored, cracked, or warped rotors affect stopping distance.
Old fluid absorbs moisture and reduces braking performance.
Anti-lock braking systems require specific diagnostic tools to verify.

items.title: Suspension & steering
items.intro: Suspension issues directly affect handling and safety at highway speeds, and are one of the most commonly missed problems in seller-provided inspections.
points: Ball joints, tie rods, and control arms
CV axle boots (watch for cracking or grease spray on surrounding surfaces)
Shock absorbers and struts
Steering rack condition

items.title: Body & frame: accident history
items.intro: A Carfax report helps but isn't the whole picture. A physical inspection can catch:
points: Uneven panel gaps (signs of bodywork after an accident)
Mismatched paint (inconsistent sheen = repainted panel)
Frame damage or previous straightening
Undercarriage rust, especially in previously-northeastern cars
outro: Get a Carfax AND a physical inspection. They catch different things.

quote.text: “Your salesperson is not your friend, your partner, or someone looking out for your best interests. They're paid on commission. The more you pay, the more they make. This doesn't mean they're evil. It just means you need to protect yourself.”

schedule.label: How to schedule a PPI
schedule.title: How to schedule a PPI.
schedule.body: Keep scrolling. The car stops at each step.

stops.title: Find your inspector first.
stops.body: Before you fall in love with a car. Having a go-to mechanic removes the pressure to scramble when you find a car you like.

stops.title: Tell the seller upfront.
stops.body: "I'd like to have this inspected by an independent mechanic before purchasing." Any seller who refuses is a red flag; walk away.

stops.title: You take the car to the mechanic.
stops.body: For private sellers, you drive it there. For dealerships, negotiate: "I'd like to take it for an extended test drive to a mechanic I've already booked." Get it in writing.

stops.title: Get the report in writing.
stops.body: Every finding, documented. No verbal summaries. You want a paper trail, for both negotiating and your own records.

stops.title: Use the findings to negotiate.
stops.body: Found a leaking CV boot? That's $300-600 in repairs. Ask the seller to reduce the price accordingly or fix it before sale.

stops.title: You can still walk away after a PPI.
stops.body: If the findings are serious and the seller won't negotiate, you didn't waste your money. You saved yourself from a much bigger loss.

alert: If a seller stalls on producing service records or promises they'll "get them later," schedule the inspection before you commit emotionally.

alert.b: Schedule the inspection before you're attached, not after.

hero.title: Know what they're doing.
hero.body: Real tactics used against buyers. Named, explained, and countered, because knowing you're being scammed is the first step to walking away.

pinkSlip.title: This document is your only proof you own the car.
pinkSlip.body: A California Certificate of Title, the "pink slip," is the legal document that proves ownership. Scroll to walk through it one section at a time.
pinkSlip.intro: Six boxes decide whether the car is really yours. Scroll to spotlight each one.

items.label: Certificate of Title
items.title: The California Certificate of Title
items.body: This is the “pink slip,” issued by the California DMV and the only legal proof that someone owns a vehicle. When you buy a car, the seller signs the back and hands it to you. You take it to the DMV to transfer it into your name. Without this step, the car is not legally yours, no matter what you paid.
items.say: If a seller says you don't need the pink slip, that they'll “mail it later,” or that it's “lost”: do not complete the purchase.

items.label: Registered Owner
items.title: Who Legally Owns This Car
items.body: The name here must match the person selling you the car. Red flags: name doesn't match the seller's ID, the registered owner is an unknown business, or the seller claims to be selling “on behalf of” someone without documentation.
items.say: Always ask for the seller's government-issued ID. The name must match the title exactly.

items.label: Vehicle History
items.title: Vehicle History: Check This First.
items.body: This box records DMV flags: salvage designation, lemon law buyback, flood damage, or prior theft recovery. A “salvage” title means the car was declared a total loss by an insurer. Both salvage and rebuilt titles dramatically affect value.
items.say: If you see any text in the Vehicle History box, research exactly what it means before proceeding.

items.label: Vehicle ID Number
items.title: The VIN Must Match Exactly.
items.body: The VIN is a unique 17-character code assigned at manufacture. Physically locate it on the car (dashboard and door jamb) and verify it matches this document character by character. A mismatch could indicate VIN cloning, where a stolen car takes the identity of a legitimate one.
items.say: Enter the VIN at vehiclehistory.gov (free) or Carfax to check accident history and title status before anything else.

items.label: Signature Section
items.title: The Seller Must Sign in Front of You.
items.body: This is where the registered owner legally releases their interest in the vehicle. This must be signed in front of you at the time of sale, not pre-signed, not signed later, not by someone other than the registered owner. A pre-signed title means someone already released ownership; you don't know to whom, or when.
items.say: Never accept: a pre-signed title, a blank signature section, or a signature from anyone other than the registered owner of record.

items.label: Odometer Disclosure
items.title: Mileage Fraud Is a Federal Crime.
items.body: Federal law requires the seller to disclose actual mileage at time of sale. Odometer rollback is a federal offense under the Motor Vehicle Information and Cost Savings Act. Verify the reading here matches the car's physical odometer, then cross-check against the vehicle history report.
items.say: If you suspect fraud: document the discrepancy with photos, do not complete the purchase, and report to NHTSA at nhtsa.gov.

flags.title: Car purchasing red flags.
flags.body: Six things dealers say, and exactly how to answer. Scroll to play each conversation.
flags.intro: Here's what you'll hear on the lot.
flags.start: Scroll to start the first conversation.

items.title: Too-Good-To-Be-True Pricing
items.body: Dealers advertise a price that already includes a stack of rebates and discounts: military, teacher, loyalty, recent grad, and more. Most buyers will not qualify for most of them. The price online is built to get you in the door, not to be the price you pay.
items.todo: Ask for the out-the-door price in writing before you go in, and ask exactly which discounts you qualify for.
items.dealer: That online price already includes every incentive we offer. You qualify for all of them, right?
items.you: Can I get the out-the-door price in writing, and exactly which discounts I qualify for?

items.title: The Disappearing Discounts
items.body: At the desk, the salesperson asks a series of qualifying questions: are you a college grad, military, a local resident, trading in a car. Each no crosses off a discount. By the end, your price has climbed by thousands, even though you were told you qualify for the manufacturer's rebate.
items.todo: Ask to see the original advertised price next to the final price, with every line item that changed and why.
items.dealer: Quick questions: military? Recent grad? Trading in a car? ...No? Okay, let me just update your price.
items.you: Show me the advertised price next to this one, with every line that changed and why.

items.title: Bogus Accessories
items.body: Wheel locks, splash guards, paint protectant, and similar add-ons get added to the price even if you never asked for them. If the dealer says it is already on the car, that is a negotiating point, not a reason to pay for it.
items.todo: Ask the dealer to remove anything you did not request, or to lower the price to reflect it.
items.dealer: The wheel locks and paint protection are already on the car, so they're part of the price.
items.you: I didn't ask for those. Take them off, or take them out of the price.

items.title: Made-Up Fees
items.body: A full tank of gas, a reconditioning fee, a CPO fee, a delivery or clean up fee: these are usually already built into the price by the manufacturer. Charging for them again is just an extra markup with an official-sounding name.
items.todo: Ask which fees are required by law and which ones are made up, then ask for those removed.
items.dealer: There's a small reconditioning fee and a delivery fee. Totally standard.
items.you: Which of these fees does the law require? Please remove the rest.

items.title: Double-Charged Destination Fee
items.body: Destination, also called freight, is already listed on the window sticker above the MSRP. A dishonest dealer will quote you a price that already includes it, then add it again later as a separate fee. If you see destination broken out on its own line, you are being charged for it twice.
items.todo: Ask whether destination is already included in the price you were quoted, and ask to see it removed if it shows up again.
items.dealer: Destination is separate. We'll add that at the end.
items.you: Was destination already in the price you quoted me? Then take the second one off.

items.title: AI-Cloned Dealers
items.body: Scammers copy a real dealership's name, website, and paperwork, often with AI-generated photos, then take payment for a car that doesn't exist. Watch for sellers who won't let you see the car in person, or who only accept an upfront wire transfer.
items.todo: Ask to see the car at the dealer's lot, or send a mobile inspector, before you pay anything.
items.dealer: We only take wire transfers. It ships tomorrow and here's your tracking link!
items.you: I'll see the car in person or send an inspector first. No wire.

yoyo.label: The yo-yo scam, animated
yoyo.title: The yo-yo scam.
yoyo.body: Also called spot delivery. Keep scrolling to watch how it plays out.
yoyo.svgLabel: A car drives from a dealership to a home, then gets pulled back to the dealership on a string

captions.text: "Congrats! Take it home today. We'll finalize your financing later."
You've shown your friends. You've traded in your old car. Then the phone rings.
"We couldn't secure your financing. You need to come back in."
A new contract with a higher rate. And your trade-in? "Already sold."
Never drive off until financing is fully approved, not "conditional." Never sign a second, worse contract.

fourSquare.title: The four-square trap.
fourSquare.body: A common way to hide the true cost of a car. Watch what happens when you ask for a lower monthly payment.
fourSquare.hidden: The part they don't write in a box
fourSquare.say: What to say: "What's the out-the-door price? I want to start there before we talk about payments."
lines: Can you get my payment lower?
Sure, let me see what I can do... $333!
Still a bit high. Any lower?
Great news: $296 a month! Sign here.
Your payment went down. Your loan went from 60 to 84 months, and you'll pay $1,761 more.

receipt.title: Read the receipt line by line.
receipt.body: Tap any charge on this sample new-car receipt. It opens right there to tell you whether the law requires it, whether you can negotiate it, or whether it's a red flag.
receipt.label: Sample dealer receipt
receipt.heading: Buyer's Order
receipt.strip: Remove everything you can say no to
receipt.saved: You just saved {amount} before negotiating the price at all.
receipt.note: Sample numbers for illustration. Tax rates and state fees vary by city and county.

lines.name: Vehicle price
lines.short: The price of the car itself.
lines.long: Everything starts here. Compare quotes from several dealers and negotiate the out-the-door price, not the monthly payment.
lines.say: "What's your best out-the-door price, in writing?"

lines.name: Destination charge
lines.short: Shipping from the factory to the dealer.
lines.long: A real manufacturer charge on new cars, and it's already printed on the window sticker. It should appear exactly once. Seeing it twice, or a second "freight" line, is a red flag.
lines.say: "The destination charge is on the sticker. Show me it's only listed once."

lines.name: Market adjustment
lines.short: Extra markup over the sticker price.
lines.long: This is pure dealer profit with no product behind it. You can refuse it, negotiate it to zero, or buy somewhere that doesn't add it.
lines.say: "I'm not paying a market adjustment. Take it off or I'll shop elsewhere."

lines.name: Dealer prep
lines.short: A charge for getting the car ready.
lines.long: Manufacturers generally pay dealers to prepare new cars for delivery, so charging you again is double-dipping.
lines.say: "Isn't prep already covered by the manufacturer? Please remove it."

lines.name: VIN etching
lines.short: The VIN etched into the windows.
lines.long: Often pre-applied and presented as mandatory. It isn't. At-home kits cost a fraction of this, and many insurers don't discount for it.
lines.say: "I didn't ask for VIN etching. Remove it from the price."

lines.name: Nitrogen-filled tires
lines.short: Nitrogen instead of air in the tires.
lines.long: Air is already about 78% nitrogen. This rarely adds meaningful value and is a common padding line.

lines.name: Paint and fabric protection
lines.long: An add-on product, not a requirement. In California, every add-on has to be listed separately with its own price, and you can decline any of them.

lines.name: Extended service contract
lines.short: Repair coverage beyond the factory warranty.
lines.long: Optional, and the price is usually negotiable. It can't be required to get financing. You can often buy one later, and from other sources.
lines.say: "I'll decline the service contract for now."

lines.name: GAP insurance
lines.short: Covers the gap if the car is totaled while you owe more than it's worth.
lines.long: Can be worth having on a big loan, but it's optional and can't be a condition of your financing. Your own insurer or credit union may sell it for less.
lines.say: "I'll get GAP through my insurer. Please remove it."

lines.name: Document fee
lines.long: California caps this fee by law. You can't usually negotiate it away, but you shouldn't pay more than the state limit.
lines.say: "Is this doc fee at or below the California cap?"

lines.name: California tire fee
lines.long: A state-mandated fee collected on each new tire sold. Small, legitimate, and required.

lines.name: Sales tax
lines.long: Required, and set by where you register the car. It's calculated on the taxable price, so every dollar you knock off the price also lowers your tax.

lines.name: Registration, title, and license fees
lines.short: Government fees paid to the DMV.
lines.long: These go to the state and are required. Ask for the itemized DMV fee breakdown and check that it matches.
lines.say: "Can I see the itemized DMV fees?"

apr.title: What a few points of APR really cost.
apr.body: The Truth in Lending Act says you get to see the APR before you sign. Drag the rate to see why that matters.
apr.overTitle: Above what the dealer can add.
apr.over: If your lender approved {buy}%, California caps the dealer's markup at {points} points on a {term}-month loan, so {cap}%. Ask to see the rate the lender approved.
apr.markupTitle: The dealer marked up your rate.
apr.markup: That costs you {amount} more in interest than the {buy}% you were approved for. It's legal up to the cap, and it's negotiable.
apr.okTitle: At or below your approved rate.
apr.ok: Getting pre-approved before you walk in is what makes this possible.

law.title: The law is already on your side.
law.body: Most buyers don't know what dealers are legally required to do. Here's what the law says, in plain English, and exactly what to say when they try to ignore it.

federal.title: Your APR must be disclosed before you sign. No exceptions.
federal.body: The dealer is required by federal law to show you your Annual Percentage Rate, the total finance charge, and the total cost of the loan before you sign anything. On a $15,000 loan, the difference between 7% APR and 30% APR is over $8,000.
federal.say: "Show me the APR, finance charge, and total of payments right now, before I sign."

federal.title: Every used car must have a Buyers Guide in the window.
federal.body: By law, every used car on a dealer lot must display a Buyers Guide sticker disclosing whether it has a warranty, what the warranty covers, or that it's sold "as is." The FTC can fine dealers up to $51,744 per missing sticker.
federal.say: No sticker visible, or a dealer who removes it before you can read it, is a federal violation. Document it.

federal.title: Odometer rollback is a federal felony.
federal.body: The dealer must provide a written odometer disclosure at the time of sale. Cross-reference the number on the contract with the physical odometer, the Carfax report, and any service records. All three must match.
federal.say: If they don't match: stop the transaction. Photograph everything. Report to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov.

federal.title: If they pull your credit, you're entitled to see exactly what they found.
federal.body: Dealers must give you a written disclosure showing your exact credit score, which bureau provided it, and how it affected your loan terms. Know your number before you walk in.
federal.say: Before you go: pull your free report at annualcreditreport.com. Walk in knowing your number.

holder.title: If you financed through the seller, your lender can be on the hook too.
holder.body: Consumer credit contracts arranged through a seller must include a notice that lets you raise the same claims against the lender that you have against the seller, up to what you've paid. When a sale turns out to be a scam, this can be what gets you out of the loan.
holder.say: Keep every receipt, message, and contract, and contact your lender in writing right away.

california.title: You can undo the purchase within 2 days, but you have to buy this right at signing.
california.body: California does not have an automatic cooling-off period. However, every licensed dealer must offer you a 2-day contract cancellation option on used cars priced $40,000 or less. It costs $75 to 1% of the purchase price plus a restocking fee if used, but it gives you a legal exit.
california.say: "I'd like to purchase the 2-day contract cancellation option."

california.title: Interest rate markups are capped. The dealer can't charge whatever they want.
california.body: California law caps dealer interest rate markups: max 2% on loans over 60 months, max 2.5% on shorter loans. Getting pre-approved at a bank or credit union before you walk in removes this leverage entirely.
california.say: Before you go: get pre-approved. Walk in with a rate. They have to beat it.

california.title: Every add-on must be listed separately with its own price. No bundling.
california.body: Any financed item must appear as a separate line item. The dealer must show your monthly payment with and without each optional item. One big bundled number presented as "the payment" is a California law violation.
california.say: "It's all just one package" isn't legal. Ask for itemized line items, in writing.

california.title: They cannot require an add-on as a condition of financing.
california.body: No dealer can require you to purchase GAP insurance, an extended warranty, paint protection, or any other add-on as a condition of getting your loan approved. If a finance manager implies you "have to" take an add-on to qualify, that's a lie, and it's illegal.
california.say: "Please show me in writing where it says this is required to get financing." Watch what happens next.

items.back: Dates, times, names. Save all texts, emails, and contracts.
Most states have consumer protection divisions for automotive fraud.
File a report at reportfraud.ftc.gov, especially for odometer fraud or a missing Buyers Guide.
